# Interviewer Guide -- Question 10: User Activity Score

**Do not share this file with candidates.**

## Source material

Real commit: `dccaa5535` -- "User Activity Score (#1119)" in the
Berkeleytime backend. Touches:

- `apps/backend/src/modules/user/jobs/activity-score-formulas.ts`
- `apps/backend/src/modules/user/jobs/update-activity-scores.ts`
- `apps/backend/src/modules/analytics/controllers/user.ts`
- `apps/backend/src/modules/analytics/resolver.ts`
- `packages/common/src/models/user.ts` (adds a single `activityScore: Number`
  field, `min: 0, max: 1`, no version tag)

The filename `activity-score-formulas.ts` is plural on purpose -- the PR
description and commit history ("created framework for testing different
formulas for user activity") show the author explicitly anticipated the
formula would be revisited, and built a `FormulaName` union + `FORMULA_MAP`
+ a single `ACTIVE_FORMULA_NAME` switch rather than hardcoding one
calculation inline. That's good instinct. Use it as the hook for Round 1:
the team already knows the formula is a moving target.

**What BT actually shipped, and its real gap (do not reveal to candidates,
use only to calibrate your own judgment during discussion):** two separate
mechanisms that don't talk to each other:

1. A nightly job (`update-activity-scores.ts`) that computes
   `ACTIVE_FORMULA` (whichever formula is currently flagged active) from
   `lastSeenAt`/`createdAt` and **overwrites** a single `activityScore`
   field on the `User` document. No version tag, no history. Switching
   `ACTIVE_FORMULA_NAME` and letting the job run again silently replaces
   every user's stored score with a new formula's output -- there is no
   record of what the old formula said.
2. A staff-dashboard comparison endpoint
   (`getActivityScoreDistribution`) that computes ALL formulas **live, on
   demand**, straight from `lastSeenAt`/`createdAt`, with no DB write. This
   works for comparing formulas *right now* only because the raw signal
   here happens to be two timestamps that don't accumulate history --
   there's no per-period signal log to replay. It genuinely cannot answer
   "how would formula B have scored users last month," because last
   month's `lastSeenAt` value isn't retained anywhere -- it's a mutable
   field, not an event log.

So BT's real system supports live formula comparison against *today's*
state, but not historical backtesting, and the precomputed field has no
versioning at all. That's exactly the gap this question is designed to
probe. A strong candidate's design should either close this gap
deliberately (and say why it's worth the cost) or explicitly flag it as an
accepted limitation.

---

## Round 1: System design discussion guide (45-60 min)

Do not tell the candidate BT's actual choice. Let them design from the
prompt in `README.md`. Below are the four defensible designs, ordered
roughly cheapest-to-priciest -- use them to calibrate, not as a checklist
requiring exact recital.

### 1. Precompute-and-store (current formula only)

A background job periodically computes the score with whatever formula is
currently "active" and writes it to a single field/column per user. Reads
are trivially cheap (indexed field read). But when the formula changes,
you either (a) leave historical values as-is, silently mixing scores
computed under different formulas with no way to tell which is which, or
(b) run a backfill to recompute everything under the new formula, which
is expensive, requires retaining enough raw signal to redo the
calculation, and permanently destroys whatever the old formula said. This
is what BT actually shipped for the single "current score" field.

### 2. Compute-on-read

Store only raw signals; compute the score live on every read using
whichever formula is current. Always consistent, zero backfill needed,
trivially supports adding new formulas (nothing to migrate). Downsides:
read cost scales with request volume and signal volume; a dashboard that
touches thousands of users on every load now runs thousands of formula
evaluations per view. Also -- and this is the sharper issue -- "historical
trend" comparisons get weird: recomputing an "old" period's score with
today's formula doesn't tell you what the system believed at the time,
only what it would believe in retrospect. If raw signals themselves are
mutable/rolling (e.g. "days since last seen" recalculated against
`Date.now()`), you may not even be able to reconstruct what the input to
the formula would have been last month. This is close to BT's staff
dashboard comparison endpoint.

### 3. Versioned snapshots

Store both the raw signals per period AND the computed score, tagged with
a formula-version identifier, so any (user, period) pair has a durable
record of what each formula said about it once it's been computed. New
formula versions are additive -- introducing one requires no migration of
past records, and comparing two formulas against the same historical
period is a straightforward query once both have been run against it, not
a live replay. The cost is a slightly bigger schema (a formula-version
column/tag) and needing to explicitly (re)run a formula against a
historical period if it wasn't run at the time -- which is fine as long as
the raw per-period signals were retained. This is the closest fit to what
BT's "multiple formulas" framework seems to be reaching for, and is the
design the starter's fixed implementation embodies.

### 4. Event-sourced signals + materialized views per formula

Append-only log of raw engagement events; one or more materialized
"current score" views maintained per formula version, updated
incrementally or recomputed on a schedule. Enables true A/B testing of
formulas against live traffic (formula A and B run in parallel, compare
which one better predicts some later outcome like re-registration).
Most powerful, by far the most infrastructure: event storage/retention
policy, materialization pipeline, view consistency/lag concerns. For a
club-sized project with a handful of engineers, this is very likely
over-engineered relative to the actual problem -- a good candidate should
be able to articulate that tradeoff explicitly, not just default to "more
sophisticated is better."

### Follow-up questions

- "The team wants to A/B test two formulas against real user data from
  last month before picking one for real. Does your design support that
  directly, or does it require replaying raw signals?" (Designs 1 and 2
  generally fail this outright or only partially; 3 supports it as long as
  raw signals for that period were retained and both formulas get run
  against them; 4 supports it natively going forward but still needs
  retained raw history to backtest against the *past*.)
- "A new engineer introduces formula C six months from now. What do they
  have to touch, and what do they NOT have to touch?" (Good answer: purely
  additive -- new formula function/version identifier, no changes to
  historical records. Red flag: anything requiring a migration of past
  data just to add a new formula.)
- "What happens if the raw signals themselves are only cheaply available
  as a rolling/mutable summary (e.g., `lastSeenAt` on the user record,
  like BT's real implementation) rather than a full per-period event log?
  Does your design still support historical backtesting, or did you
  implicitly assume event-level signal retention that doesn't actually
  exist?" This is worth pushing on -- it's exactly where BT's real system
  quietly falls short.

### Red flags

- Designs a single hardcoded formula with no acknowledgment that it will
  change -- misses the entire premise of the prompt.
- Never addresses what happens to already-computed historical scores when
  the formula changes at all (doesn't distinguish "leave them stale,"
  "backfill them," or "version them" as different, consequential choices).
- Claims compute-on-read gives "full historical accuracy" without noticing
  that raw signals must actually be retained per-period for that to be
  true -- conflates "no backfill needed" with "can answer any historical
  question," which isn't the same thing unless the signal storage
  supports it.
- Jumps straight to design 4 (event sourcing + materialized views) without
  being asked, and can't explain why that complexity is justified for this
  problem's actual scale.

## Round 2: Code review guide

### What the tests verify (`impl/test/activity-scores.test.ts`)

`src/scoring.ts` ships as a stub -- both `computeActivityScores` and
`getActivityScore` throw `"not implemented"`, so all 7 tests fail
immediately on the unmodified starter. That's expected; it's not
diagnostic of anything. What matters is what each test verifies about a
CORRECT implementation, and which ones a shallow implementation is likely
to get wrong:

1. **Baseline correctness (two tests)** -- `weightedV1` and `weightedV2`
   each compute the right score for a period, checked against
   hand-computed expected values. Any reasonable implementation that
   actually calls `FORMULA_MAP[formulaVersion]` per signal will pass these
   -- they confirm the formula is wired up, not that versioning works.
2. **Non-destruction** -- running `computeActivityScores` with
   `weightedV2` for a period must leave whatever `weightedV1` previously
   computed for that same period completely untouched. This is the crux
   of the exercise: an implementation that stores one record per (userId,
   period), without the formula version as part of the storage identity,
   fails this immediately -- the second call overwrites the first.
3. **Independent retrieval of both formulas** -- after running both
   formulas for a period, `getActivityScore(..., "weightedV1")` and
   `getActivityScore(..., "weightedV2")` must return their own distinct
   results. This is the same requirement as #2, checked from the read
   side: you must be able to ask "what did formula X say about this
   period" for either formula, after the fact, regardless of which one ran
   most recently.
4. **Same-formula re-run updates only its own record** -- re-running
   `weightedV1` for a period should update `weightedV1`'s own stored
   record without touching `weightedV2`'s record for that same period.
   This distinguishes "versioned by formula" from a naive fix that just
   never overwrites anything (e.g. append-only with no way to update a
   stale run of the same formula).
5. **Unknown combination returns undefined**, and **both periods' results
   stay independently retrievable across formulas** -- broader checks that
   the versioning generalizes across more than one period, not just the
   two-formula/one-period happy path.

A correct implementation touches `src/scoring.ts` only; it does not
require touching `types.ts`, `formulas.ts`, or `fixtures.ts`. One correct
approach -- described here as one option among several, not the only
right answer:

```ts
const scoreStore = new Map<string, ActivityScoreRecord>();

const storeKey = (
  userId: string,
  period: string,
  formulaVersion: FormulaName
): string => `${userId}|${period}|${formulaVersion}`;

export const computeActivityScores = (
  formulaVersion: FormulaName,
  period: string,
  signals: EngagementSignals[]
): ActivityScoreRecord[] => {
  const formula = FORMULA_MAP[formulaVersion];
  const periodSignals = signals.filter((s) => s.period === period);

  const records: ActivityScoreRecord[] = periodSignals.map((s) => ({
    userId: s.userId,
    period,
    formulaVersion,
    score: formula(s),
    computedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  }));

  for (const record of records) {
    scoreStore.set(storeKey(record.userId, record.period, record.formulaVersion), record);
  }

  return records;
};

export const getActivityScore = (
  userId: string,
  period: string,
  formulaVersion: FormulaName
): ActivityScoreRecord | undefined => {
  return scoreStore.get(storeKey(userId, period, formulaVersion));
};

export const _resetStoreForTests = (): void => {
  scoreStore.clear();
};
```

The change from a naive first attempt (keying by `userId|period` alone) is
just adding `formulaVersion` to the storage key. Equally valid: a nested
`Map<string, Map<FormulaName, ActivityScoreRecord>>`, or an array filtered
on read. Judge on correctness and clarity, not the exact data structure.

### AI-tool-usage questions to ask

- "Walk me through your first prompt, and what came back." A candidate
  working from a solid Round 1 design should be steering the AI toward
  versioned storage from the start. Ask directly: "did the AI's first
  draft account for multiple formula versions coexisting in storage on
  its own, or did you have to point out that requirement yourself?" Both
  answers are fine, but they should know which happened -- someone who
  can't say suggests they weren't reading the output critically.
- "Did the AI suggest a fix that changed `types.ts`, `formulas.ts`, or the
  test file? What did you do with that suggestion?" (Good candidates catch
  and reject suggestions that would edit the fixed files/spec instead of
  `scoring.ts`.)
- "Show me the prompt log." Look for whether they iterated when the first
  attempt didn't fully pass, or accepted something and moved on without
  checking `npm test` again.

### Red flags

- Implementation overwrites historical scores in place with no way to
  recover what a previous formula said for a given period -- i.e., they
  built exactly the single-slot-per-period storage the exercise is meant
  to steer them away from. Ask them to trace through what happens with a
  hypothetical `weightedV3` to check the design actually generalizes.
- Cannot explain, when asked directly, "what would you tell someone doing
  a formula A/B test with your system?" -- if they can't articulate that
  their implementation lets you retrieve either formula's answer for a
  shared period, they may have pattern-matched their way to passing tests
  without understanding why the tests check what they check.
- Deletes or weakens assertions in the test file to make it pass (a hard
  stop -- the instructions explicitly say not to edit the test file).
- Can't distinguish, when asked, between "the formula changed" and "the
  raw signals changed" as two different reasons a stored score might
  become stale -- conflating these suggests they haven't internalized why
  versioning by formula specifically (not just re-running periodically)
  matters.

## Rubric (1-5 each)

| Dimension | 1 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| System design judgment | Hardcodes one formula, ignores the "will change" premise | Picks a reasonable design, some gaps in backfill/read-cost reasoning | Picks a design, correctly reasons about read cost vs. backfill cost vs. historical comparability, and is explicit about what raw signal retention their design assumes |
| Code quality/correctness | Fix is a hack that passes tests without fixing the actual key collision | Fix works, storage approach is workable but a bit awkward | Fix is clean, generalizes past the specific fixtures/tests, and the resulting types/API read naturally |
| Tradeoff articulation | Can't explain why their design gives up anything | Can name the tradeoff of their chosen design when asked | Proactively states what their design gives up vs. the alternatives, unprompted |
| AI-tool usage judgment | Accepted first suggestion without checking it fixed the real bug (or edited tests/fixtures to force a pass) | Used the tool productively, caught at least one bad suggestion | Iterated deliberately, can point to exactly where they verified vs. where they trusted output, log reflects real back-and-forth |
| Communication | Rambles, can't answer the "what would you tell an A/B tester" question | Explains design clearly when prompted | Proactively frames the historical-comparison question as the crux of the problem, without being led there |

## Time budget

- Round 1: 45-60 min system design discussion, no code.
- Round 2: 3-4 hour slot -- expect ~1-2 hours of actual implementation
  time, remainder for code review discussion and AI-tool-usage debrief.
